title: The Two Density Modes of A/16
takeaway: Plotting how often each learned feature fires, on a log axis, splits the features of run A/16 into two humps: a spike of features that fire on roughly one token in ten million, and a broad bulk centred near one token in a hundred thousand. The paper reports that almost all of the right-hand features are interpretable and almost none of the left-hand ones are, and treats the left hump — which it names the ultralow density cluster — as a suspected artifact of autoencoder training rather than anything in the transformer.
walkthrough:
You are looking at one chart that summarises a whole [[dictionary-learning-run]]. The run is A/16, one of the ninety [[sparse-autoencoder]]s the paper trained on the same one-layer transformer. Every learned [[feature]] in that run contributes one count to one bar, so the chart is a census of the dictionary rather than a picture of any single feature.

The x axis is [[feature-density]]: the fraction of tokens in the training set on which a feature has a nonzero activation. It is plotted as $\log_{10}$ of that fraction. The tick at $-7$ therefore means a density of $10^{-7}$, one token in ten million; the tick at $-2$ means one token in a hundred. Note where that leaves the whole chart — even the busiest feature shown is silent on more than 99% of tokens.

The y axis is a plain count of features per bin. The tallest bar says roughly 7,500 features sit in the bin nearest $10^{-7}$.

Now the shape. Two humps make the histogram bimodal, which the paper says is typical rather than peculiar to this run. The left hump is drawn in purple and labelled "Ultra Low Density Cluster". The right hump is the grey mass, peaking around $10^{-5}$ and thinning out past $10^{-3}$; the paper calls it the [[high-density-cluster]], while noting that the name is relative and the density there is still very low.

The split matters because the two humps behave differently. Anecdotally, the paper says, almost every feature in the right hump is interpretable and almost none in the left hump is. It reads the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] as an artifact of autoencoder training, not a property of the transformer; those units fire so seldom that they are [[de-facto-dead-neurons]], invisible to a plain count of [[dead-neurons]]. In the smaller run A/1, 292 of 4,096 features fell below one in a million and were dropped from later analyses.

Two hedges travel with the figure. The right mode may itself be two modes, near $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-3}$, which the authors say they are still investigating. And the clean gap here does not always appear: for wide dictionaries with a large [[l1-coefficient]] the clusters overlap, and separating them then needs extra statistics.

terms.definition: Names what is being counted (feature density) and which trained dictionary the features come from (run A/16). Every bar in the chart belongs to that single run.

An identifier for one dictionary learning run under the paper's naming scheme: 'A' is the transformer the activations came from, and '16' indexes one of the autoencoders trained on it, each with its own dictionary size and sparsity penalty. The paper keeps a separate table of runs; the text here does not restate A/16's size or L1 coefficient.

The horizontal position of a feature is the base-10 logarithm of its density, so each unit step to the right is a tenfold increase in how often the feature fires. The log scale is what makes both the $10^{-7}$ spike and the $10^{-3}$ tail visible on one chart.

The paper's definition: the fraction of tokens on which a given feature has a nonzero activation. It is used as a cheap proxy for autoencoder quality during iteration, not as a measure of anything the feature means.
The number of features whose density falls in that histogram bin. It counts features, not tokens and not activations.

terms.term: Ultra Low Density Cluster (purple annotation and purple bars)
terms.definition: The left mode, made of features that fire on around one token in ten million. The paper reports that almost none of these are interpretable and suspects they are an artifact of the autoencoder training process rather than a real property of the transformer.

terms.term: High density cluster (the grey mass, unlabelled in the image)
terms.definition: The right mode, named in the surrounding text rather than on the chart. The paper says almost all of its features are interpretable, and points out that the name is comparative: an absolute density near $10^{-5}$ is still very rare firing.
Having two separated peaks. Here it means the dictionary's features do not sit on one smooth spread of densities but fall into two distinguishable populations.

One narrow interval of $\log_{10}$ density; the bar's height is how many features landed in it. Because binning is done in log space, each bar covers a fixed ratio of densities rather than a fixed difference.

An autoencoder hidden unit with zero activation across a large number of datapoints. Such units are counted separately and would not appear anywhere on this chart, since their density is zero and has no logarithm.

The paper's description of ultralow density units: alive by the strict test, since they do fire occasionally, but so rare that they contribute nothing usable. This is why the paper prefers counting the high density cluster over counting dead neurons.

The scalar weighting the sparsity penalty against reconstruction error in the autoencoder's loss. It is not shown on this chart, but it matters for reading it: with a large coefficient and many autoencoder neurons, the paper says the two clusters stop separating cleanly.

numbers.meaning: The x axis ticks, in $\log_{10}$ of density. They correspond to one activation per 10 million tokens, per million, per 100,000, per 10,000, per 1,000 and per 100 respectively. The axis stops near $-7$ on the left because that is about the rarest firing the paper can estimate, and near $-2$ on the right because no feature in this run is busier than roughly one token in a few hundred.
The centre of the left mode, stated in the text. A feature there fires on about one token in ten million.
The centre of the right mode, stated in the text. A feature there fires on about one token in a hundred thousand — the paper's point that the 'high density cluster' is high only by comparison.
The location of a possible second peak inside the right mode, which the paper flags in a note and says it is still investigating. About one token in a thousand.
The y axis ticks, in features per bin. The scale reaching into the thousands is itself informative: a dictionary this large has tens of thousands of features in total.
The height of the tallest purple bar, at the far left. It is the single most populated density bin in the run, and all of it sits in the cluster the paper distrusts.

The heights of the successive purple bars moving right from the spike. Each is roughly half the one before, so the ultralow cluster is a sharp peak with a short decaying shoulder, not a broad population.
The plateau height of the grey mass between roughly $10^{-5.5}$ and $10^{-4}$. Spread over dozens of bins, this is where the bulk of the run's usable features live.

The transformer's MLP width and the largest autoencoder width the paper trains, from its setup table — an expansion of 256×, against the 8× expansion used for the main run. A/16's own width is not given in the text, but bar counts totalling tens of thousands place it well up that range.
The number of learned dictionaries the paper trained and published visualizations for. A/16 is one of them, and the appendix shows density histograms for all the Seed A runs.

For the smaller run A/1, the number of learned features, the number that are dead (active on none of 100 million dataset examples), and the number classed as ultralow density. Both latter groups are excluded from the paper's later analyses. The 292 is about 7% of the dictionary; the numbers are quoted here because the paper gives no equivalent breakdown for A/16.
The density threshold the paper uses in its global analysis to call a feature ultralow. On this chart that is the tick at $-6$, which falls just right of where the purple bars end.

The number of dataset examples over which A/1's feature activity was checked. A count of this order is what lets densities as small as $10^{-7}$ be estimated at all, since a feature at that density fires on only about ten of them.

The activation vectors used for autoencoder training out of the collected dataset, sampled without replacement over 1 million steps. It sets the scale of 'training set' in the definition of feature density.
